notes.b: The heart does not wait for instructions to beat. A small patch of muscle in its own wall sets the pace and sends a wave of electrical signals that makes the chambers contract in the right order.
points: A heartbeat is one contraction and relaxation of the heart muscle, pumping blood out of the ventricles (the two lower chambers) into the arteries.
An adult heart beats about 70 times a minute at rest, a normal resting range being about 60 to 100, and it does so every minute of life.

Cardiac muscle (heart muscle) is myogenic: the beat starts within the heart muscle itself, without a nerve impulse. This is why a heart removed for transplant keeps beating for a time if it is supplied with oxygenated fluid.

The pacemaker is the sinoatrial node (SA node), a small patch of specialised cardiac muscle in the wall of the right atrium (an upper chamber), near where the superior vena cava (the large vein from the upper body) enters.
The SA node produces electrical impulses at regular intervals by itself. Each impulse starts one heartbeat, so the SA node sets the rate of the heartbeat.
notes.tip: If asked to name the pacemaker and give its location, answer the SA node in the wall of the right atrium, not the left and not the brain. To explain how it controls the heartbeat, say it makes impulses by itself and each impulse starts one beat.

notes.h: How the impulse spreads through the heart
notes.b: The impulse from the SA node does not reach every part at once. It travels in a set route with a built-in pause, which makes the atria contract first and the ventricles second.
points: 1. The impulse from the SA node spreads across the walls of both atria, so the atria contract together, pushing blood into the ventricles.
2. A layer of non-conducting tissue between the atria and the ventricles stops the impulse passing straight to the ventricles, so the ventricles cannot contract too early.

3. The impulse reaches the atrioventricular node (AV node), at the base of the right atrium near the septum (the wall between the two sides of the heart). The AV node delays it for a fraction of a second, giving the atria time to empty into the ventricles.
4. The AV node passes the impulse down conducting fibres in the septum (the bundle of His) to the apex (the pointed lower tip of the heart), and then up through the ventricle walls (Purkinje fibres).

5. The ventricles contract from the apex upwards, squeezing blood up into the aorta and pulmonary artery, the two arteries leaving the heart. The atria therefore contract before the ventricles, and the two sides beat together.

Diagram: a front-view outline of the heart showing the SA node in the wall of the right atrium, the AV node near the septum, the conducting fibres down the septum and up the ventricle walls, with arrows for the spread of the impulse.

notes.b: The SA node sets a basic rhythm, but the body's needs change from moment to moment. Nerves and a hormone adjust the rate the SA node sets, so the heart can speed up or slow down.
points: The rate is changed to match the body's needs. It rises during exercise, because the muscles then need more oxygen and glucose and produce more CO₂, which the faster-flowing blood delivers and carries away.

Nervous control: the cardiac centre in the medulla oblongata (part of the brainstem) sends impulses along two sets of nerves to the SA node. One set, the sympathetic nerves, speeds up the heart rate; the other, the vagus nerve, a parasympathetic nerve, slows it down.
The medulla responds to information from receptors, which detect changes in the body. For example, a rise in CO₂ in the blood increases heart rate, and a rise in blood pressure slows it.
Hormonal control: adrenaline, released by the adrenal glands in stress, danger or excitement, acts on the SA node and increases the heart rate and the force of contraction.

Other factors that change heart rate include exercise and fitness, age (higher in babies and children), body temperature (a fever raises it), emotion, caffeine and nicotine, which raise it, and some medicines.

Artificial pacemaker: if the SA node fails, or the impulse does not reach the ventricles properly (heart block), the heart beats too slowly or irregularly. A small battery-powered device is implanted under the skin below the collarbone, with a wire, or lead, running through a vein into the heart.

The artificial pacemaker detects the heart's own rhythm and sends an electrical impulse to start a beat when one is missed or the rate is too slow. The batteries last several years and are replaced in a minor operation.
notes.tip: Learn which way each control acts: the vagus nerve slows the heart, while sympathetic nerves and adrenaline speed it up. The brain only changes the rate set by the SA node; the heart would still beat without it.

notes.b: Each time the ventricles contract, they force a surge of blood into the arteries. You can feel this surge as the pulse, which gives an easy way to measure heart rate.
points: The pulse is a wave of expansion of an artery wall, caused by the surge of blood forced into the arteries each time the ventricles contract. The stretched elastic wall then recoils. The pulse rate therefore equals the heart rate.

The pulse can be felt where an artery runs close to the skin over a bone or firm tissue. The usual sites are the radial artery at the wrist, on the thumb side, and the carotid artery in the neck, beside the windpipe.
Veins have no pulse, because the pressure wave has been lost in the capillaries (the tiny vessels between arteries and veins) before the blood reaches them.
Method for measuring pulse: 1. Sit quietly for a few minutes, so the reading is a resting one.
2. Press lightly with the index and middle fingers, not the thumb, which has its own pulse, on the radial artery.
3. Count the beats for 30 seconds and double the number to give beats per minute, or count for a full 60 seconds.
4. Repeat three times and take the mean, which reduces the effect of any one miscount.
If asked what the pulse is, say it is a wave in the artery wall, not blood flowing past your finger.
notes.tip: Remember that pulse rate equals heart rate, that veins have no pulse, and that you use the fingers, never the thumb.

notes.b: Exercise makes the muscles need more oxygen, so the heart speeds up. Measuring the pulse before and after exercise shows this, and how quickly it recovers shows how fit someone is.
points: This is a standard class investigation with primary data (data you collect yourself). Measure the resting pulse; exercise, for example with step-ups for two minutes; then measure the pulse at once and every minute until it returns to the resting value.
The pulse rises during exercise and falls gradually afterwards. The time taken to return to the resting rate, the recovery time, is shorter in fitter people.
Fitter people also tend to have a lower resting pulse, because each beat pumps more blood.
Independent variable (the one you change): activity level (rest, or after exercise). Dependent variable (the one you measure): pulse rate in beats per minute.
Controlled variables (kept the same): the type, duration and intensity of the exercise, the same person, the same counting method and the same posture.
notes.tip: For the effect of exercise on pulse rate, give the rise during exercise and the gradual fall afterwards, and name the independent and dependent variables correctly.

notes.b: Blood only flows round the body because the ventricles push it with force. That force, pressing on the walls of the vessels, is blood pressure, and when it stays too high it harms the body.
points: Blood pressure is the force that the blood exerts on the walls of the blood vessels, produced by the contraction of the ventricles.
Pressure is highest in the aorta and large arteries, falls as blood passes through the arterioles (small arteries) and capillaries, and is lowest in the veins and venae cavae.
Measurement: a sphygmomanometer, or blood pressure monitor, uses an inflatable cuff on the upper arm over the brachial artery. Pressure is given in millimetres of mercury (mmHg).

Pressure is given as two numbers: the higher pressure, when the ventricles contract, and the lower pressure, when the heart relaxes between beats. A healthy young adult at rest has a value of about 120/80 mmHg.
Blood pressure rises naturally during exercise or stress and falls during sleep. High blood pressure, or hypertension, means a resting value consistently at or above about 140/90 mmHg.
Hypertension usually has no symptoms, but it strains the heart, damages artery walls and raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney damage.
Factors that raise blood pressure include too much salt in the diet, being overweight, lack of exercise, smoking, too much alcohol, stress, older age and family history.
High blood pressure is controlled by lifestyle changes, such as less salt, exercise, weight loss and not smoking, and by medication.
notes.tip: Exams ask what blood pressure is, how it is measured and the risks of high blood pressure. Give the instrument (sphygmomanometer), the unit (mmHg) and the two numbers, and name heart attack, stroke and kidney damage as the risks.

notes.b: The heart works non-stop, so its muscle needs a steady supply of oxygen and glucose. It cannot get these from the blood inside its chambers, so it has a separate circulation of its own.
points: The heart muscle cannot take oxygen and nutrients from the blood passing through its chambers: the wall is too thick for diffusion to reach most cells, and the blood on the left side passes too quickly. So the heart has its own circulation, the coronary circulation.

The two coronary arteries, left and right, are the first branches of the aorta, arising from its base just above the aortic semilunar valve (the valve at the exit of the left ventricle). They run over the surface of the heart, branching into smaller arteries that enter the muscle.

These small arteries supply a dense network of capillaries. This gives the cardiac muscle the oxygen and glucose for the aerobic respiration (energy release using oxygen) that keeps it working continuously.

Deoxygenated blood from the heart muscle is collected by the cardiac (coronary) veins, which run over the surface and join a large vein at the back of the heart, the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.
Diagram: a front view of the heart showing the aorta, the left and right coronary arteries branching from its base and running over the surface, and the cardiac veins. Label each.
notes.tip: The coronary arteries branch from the aorta, not the pulmonary artery, and run on the outside of the heart. If asked why the heart needs its own blood supply, say the wall is too thick for diffusion from the chambers.

notes.b: The coronary arteries are narrow, so damage to them has serious effects. When they narrow or block, the heart muscle is starved of oxygen.
points: Fatty deposits, called atheroma or plaque and containing cholesterol, can build up in the walls of the coronary arteries and narrow them (atherosclerosis), so less blood reaches the heart muscle. This can cause chest pain during exercise, called angina.
If a blood clot forms on a damaged plaque and blocks a coronary artery, the part of the heart muscle that it supplies is starved of oxygen and dies. This is a heart attack, or myocardial infarction.
Clot-dissolving enzymes given soon after a heart attack can break down the clot and restore blood flow to the starved muscle, so they limit the damage (see 'Industrial enzymes').
Risk factors: smoking, a diet high in saturated fat, which raises blood cholesterol, high blood pressure, obesity, lack of exercise, diabetes, older age and family history.
Prevention: not smoking, a balanced diet, regular exercise and a healthy weight, which each remove a risk factor.

Technology: a narrowed coronary artery can be widened by angioplasty, in which a balloon on a catheter (a thin tube) is inflated inside the artery and a small mesh tube, a stent, is left in place to hold it open.
Alternatively, the narrowed artery can be bypassed by a coronary artery bypass graft, using a piece of vein, often from the leg, or an artery to carry blood around the blockage.
notes.tip: If asked what causes a heart attack, link it in order: plaque narrows the coronary artery, a clot blocks it, and the heart muscle it supplies is starved of oxygen and dies.

keyTerms.definition: The sinoatrial node, a patch of specialised cardiac muscle in the wall of the right atrium that produces regular impulses and sets the heart rate.
The node at the base of the right atrium that delays the impulse before it passes to the ventricles.
Conducting fibres in the septum that carry the impulse from the AV node down to the apex of the heart.
Conducting fibres in the ventricle walls that carry the impulse up from the apex, so the ventricles contract from the bottom upwards.
Describes heart muscle that starts each beat within itself, without a nerve impulse.
The wave of expansion of an artery wall, caused by the surge of blood when the ventricles contract.
A device with an inflatable cuff that measures blood pressure in mmHg.
High blood pressure, meaning a resting value consistently at or above about 140/90 mmHg.
The arteries that branch from the base of the aorta and supply the heart muscle with blood.
The large vein at the back of the heart that collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium.
A fatty deposit, containing cholesterol, that builds up in the wall of an artery and narrows it.
Chest pain during exercise caused by reduced blood supply to the heart muscle.
A heart attack, in which part of the heart muscle dies because a coronary artery is blocked.
A procedure in which a balloon on a catheter is inflated inside a narrowed artery, and a stent is left in place to hold it open.
